issue.body:
Related: #196662

**Maintainer decision: land on the counterbalanced pilot evidence. Final measurement acceptance remains pending because shared-host contention and unstable A/A controls prevented a qualified full campaign.**

## What Problem This Solves

Taking and recursively removing a full btrfs snapshot on every changed command reduced container pauses but added 28% command latency and CPU in the original 62,000-file benchmark. Small workspaces should not pay that snapshot cost.

## User Impact

Small, fast checkpoints keep direct paused capture. Expensive checkpoints retain atomic capture and resume before scanning. Commands still wait for canonical acceptance; after runtime resume, the workspace lease renames the disposable capture to a unique retired path and hands cleanup to the existing run-end lifetime. The next command can execute during deletion; the next snapshot waits for pending cleanup and retries interrupted removals before creating another artifact.

Cleanup keeps the existing native recursive remover and needs no new utility, privilege or mount option. Snapshot creation can still wait for dirty writeback, and nested subvolumes retain the complete paused fallback.

## Why This Change Was Made

The manifest worker already knows the accepted entry count. It now carries that fact on an early-aborting probe, so a large tree is recognized even when the changed pathname sorts first. A 20,000-entry inventory or a probe lasting 500 ms selects snapshots. No additional scan, persistent cache, schema, or configuration is introduced. Recovery and initial layout capture without probe facts remain on the direct path.

Canonical writes retain session authority. The lease transfers only an immutable, disposable artifact to independent cleanup. Unique retired names prevent delayed deletion from touching a later capture. Pending promises track active work, not cached scan results; persistent removal failures prevent another snapshot from growing the backlog. A rolling snapshot cannot be refreshed by the current immutable-copy primitive, and an early probe is not a complete changed-path set for safe selective reflinks.

The snapshot manifest scan also avoids one asynchronous filesystem dispatch per metadata read inside the existing capture worker. A shared 32-read yield services cancellation; the main thread and non-snapshot scans retain asynchronous reads. File hashing, identity and containment checks are unchanged.

## Evidence

Two regressions fail on the parent: small btrfs checkpoints unnecessarily invoke snapshots, and completed commands remain blocked behind capture deletion. On the candidate all 9 checkpoint scenarios pass, including interrupted acceptance, nested fallback, later guest writes, canonical read-after-command, bounded cleanup custody and caller disposal. Native filesystem owner tests: 10/10. The broader projection owner run passed 83 tests with 2 platform skips; its one obsolete always-snapshot recovery expectation was corrected and replayed green.

The next-command overlap regressions additionally fail on preliminary head a04f5a346a0db94ff634fc0d5969edee4e729ba3 with `OPENCLAW_STATE_LEASE_HELD`, then pass on the retired-path handoff. Final staged candidate Codex autoreview is scoped-clean through P2. Production delta: +125 LOC: 103 for adaptive capture and bounded lifetime transfer/recovery, plus 22 for worker metadata reads. Tests: +205 LOC, including real-worker scan equivalence and cooperative cancellation; the two scanner/worker test files pass all 45 tests. The checkpoint test registrations move to their existing fixture module to stay within the file limit without dropping coverage.

`pnpm check:changed --base 4ec97ef5e73e0780cb0d9a70d096a1bba5600027` completed on the final candidate: all categories pass except the inherited unused-export scans. Both reproduce on the exact parent with identical 28/8 symbol sets and attributed introducing commits. These are existing main regressions. The runtime build also passes. The nine checkpoint cases take 57.24 s including cold compilation (54.17 s Vitest duration, 63% transform and 35% tests); they exercise the actual SQLite lease and lifecycle boundary. The maintainer explicitly accepted the pilot for landing; the incomplete final native campaign remains a measurement limitation, not completed proof.

The exact 205 regression lines have a justified allocation record, and the test-line guard passes against the branch parent. Final-head CI run `42859153410` passes every job except baseline-ratchets and its dependent CI gate. The exact CI main parent `ecbad2efa1d7e89d041965612b2237760a024c50` independently reproduces 18 lines of debt: 6,632,310 test lines against a 6,632,292 ceiling. #196680 (`3686da563c54738b11fac5c9a103ee8b3943b5e6`) introduced 21 lines of debt; #196636 and #196742 paid down three. This PR adds 205 test lines and 205 credit, leaving the inherited debt unchanged. This remains a named main regression.

Final-head CodeQL and OpenGrep initially completed analysis but failed while uploading SARIF because of GitHub installation API rate limits. Only those failed jobs were rerun after diagnosis; both workflows succeeded on attempt 2. No security exception or alert dismissal was used. ClawSweeper reviewed the final source head and reports zero findings.

### Native measurement acceptance, recorded before the campaign

Final performance results are pending. The first complete adaptive/cleanup campaign passed small-workspace latency and large pause goals, but did not establish a CPU improvement over the snapshot-every-command implementation, so it was held. A counterbalanced 20-command metadata pilot reduced command median from 2623 to 2088 ms and cgroup CPU from 4694 to 3346 ms/command; snapshot scan time fell from 1517 to 999 ms. All read checks passed. These are pilot results, not the final acceptance campaign.

The first final-head small campaign was affected by another benchmark becoming active in the shared Docker VM. All consistency checks passed, but the whole attempt is retained as contended evidence, not performance acceptance. Subsequent quiet 10/10 controls still differed by 24.7% in command median, despite only 4.6% CPU variation. Recorded phases place most variation in command/engine control and staging waits; manifest scan stayed at 23 ms. Those controls are retained. One explicitly recorded small-workspace protocol revision uses the unchanged driver with 10 warmup and 50 measured commands per arm (`--requests 5`), improving sample resolution without assuming a warmup cause. The large protocol stays 10/10; outcome targets are unchanged. The revised first control passed correctness but failed its independent resource gate: another workload consumed 34.43 CPU-seconds and 563.85 MB reads during 60.22 seconds. No second control or paired campaign followed. All native timing is now idle pending a reserved quiet interval; no favorable subset or repeated-until-green controls will be selected.

The selected runtime and extended worker-allocation driver are pinned to `12227a56a740261516bb036efcad77fa8078837f`. Fresh full-candidate Codex autoreview is scoped-clean through P2; runtime build, targeted checks and the 205-line test allocation pass. The maintainer accepted the pilot for landing at this exact head under the review/security gates and the documented inherited-CI exception. Pilot command median 2.09 s is below the earlier pre-#196662 baseline of 2.37 s, but that comparison is across campaigns, not a qualified final paired comparison. Pilot pause p95 is 223 ms, cgroup CPU improves 28.7%, and all consistency checks pass. Shared-host noise leaves final two-regime acceptance, worker allocation and writeback diagnostics pending. The committed driver is `scripts/perf/local-workspace-checkpoint-measure.ts`; writeback diagnostics use `scripts/perf/local-workspace-snapshot-writeback.py`.

Use real Podman+btrfs, 62,000 files/1.1 GB and 100 files/400 KiB, with the same approximately 35 GiB synthetic agent database and 10,000 sessions. Compare pre-#196662 source 3f17d921f6cc1cf03d52054a74ba3a5e885f5c35, shipped 10d67445fbecbc3c25f9bb5a5020766e3513b64b, and this pinned candidate. Each large formal arm has 10 warm-up and 10 measured mutating commands; the revised small arms have 10 warm-up and 50 measured commands, with canonical and next-guest read checks throughout. Run A/A controls and five counterbalanced baseline/candidate pairs per regime; retain slow and failed arms.

Small-workspace command median must match or improve the pre-change baseline within measured A/A spread, with zero snapshots. Large-workspace pause p95 must be at most 300 ms, with command latency and total CPU materially below the snapshot-every-command implementation. Report remaining differences from the pre-change baseline explicitly. No 20% latency/CPU regression is accepted implicitly.

Include the final cleanup tail outside per-command latency but inside burst CPU/wall accounting. Wait for btrfs kernel deletion work and report whole-VM CPU as well as cgroup CPU, since kernel cleaner work can escape container accounting. Measure allocation separately and keep instrumented profiles out of plain latency results. Dirty-writeback tests compare source churn at 1.7 GB/hour, explicit pre-syncfs, and separately labeled 1.1 GB bursts; they cannot retrospectively attribute an untraced historical pause.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes slow managed-worktree dependency provisioning when a long-running Gateway has a large resident address space, even though native copy-on-write copying is available.

Related: #196298, #196390, #193090, #191873.

## User Impact

Large dependency includes stay fast as Gateway memory grows. File selection, independent copied contents, timestamps, existing-destination protection, live authority, and cancellation retain their contracts. No configuration, cache, schema, or dependency change is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The filesystem worker is a thread in the Gateway process. Forking GNU `cp` once per 128-file batch therefore copies the large process's page tables hundreds of times. The earlier small-process benchmark missed that cost.

Use one operation-owned small helper to run the same bounded native batches. Its inherited procfs directory descriptor resolves the parent's retained source/staging descriptors; requests contain only numeric descriptors. Each accepted batch settles before cleanup, and fresh host authority still gates publication after the awaited copy. Capability failure selects the portable copier before traversal; failed accepted work is never replayed through fallback.

The existing preparation receipt gains bounded `copyDetails`: copier/fallback reason, admitted source bytes, batch count, large-parent helper spawn count/time, child wait time, and authority count/time. These aggregates contain no file paths or contents. `sourceBytes` is logical content size, not physical IO; child and authority timings are not additive to the overall phase. This extends the existing receipt boundary also used by #193090, without adding another log family or changing its wait/copy phase split.

## Evidence

The acceptance rule was recorded before candidate measurement: 65,880 selected files / 1.647 GB, including nested dependency directories; Node 24.22.1, uid 1000, jemalloc, 8 GiB touched parent memory, btrfs with compression; serial baseline/candidate pairs with fresh destinations, at least 5× lower wall time and large-parent forks, Gateway copy below 10 seconds, and identical bytes/mode/nanosecond mtime/paths plus source independence and shared extents. CPU/allocation must not materially regress.

Five interleaved owner pairs on Linux ARM64 (all samples retained):

| Pair | Baseline wall | Candidate wall | Baseline CPU¹ | Candidate CPU¹ | Baseline allocation² | Candidate allocation² |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 41.361 s | 4.084 s | 41.648 s | 4.005 s | 237.7 MB | 206.3 MB |
| 2 | 44.215 s | 5.491 s | 43.842 s | 5.124 s | 242.3 MB | 208.8 MB |
| 3 | 48.839 s | 4.679 s | 48.497 s | 4.577 s | 245.1 MB | 207.4 MB |
| 4 | 63.282 s | 9.692 s | 55.347 s | 6.770 s | 242.9 MB | 202.9 MB |
| 5 | 44.464 s | 5.707 s | 44.289 s | 5.172 s | 249.7 MB | 210.4 MB |

**Medians:** wall 44.464 → 5.491 s (**8.10×**), CPU 44.289 → 5.124 s (**−88.4%**), allocation 242.9 → 207.4 MB (**−14.6%**). The 515 asynchronous data-copy spawns from the large parent become one helper spawn; median time spent synchronously inside those spawn calls is 39.586 s → 84.85 ms. Baseline also has one synchronous GNU cp capability probe, included in wall/CPU but outside the 515 asynchronous-spawn count; the candidate performs its probe inside the small helper. All runs retain 515 bounded native batches and verify all 65,880 selected files, exact modes/nanosecond mtimes/path set, exclusions, source independence, and zero exclusive btrfs bytes.

¹ CPU includes the process and settled descendants. ² Node 24 allocation is sampled V8 allocation including collected objects, not an exact counter. Measured runtime/harness sources are pinned at `25a9a732`, baseline `ecbad2ef`; the final head changes tests/accounting and integrates disjoint main changes, with identical copier/harness/dependency inputs.

A/A baseline controls were 75.753, 44.528, and 36.428 s. The first overlapped repository review/check reads; peer builds also heavily contended the shared Mac, which guest load averages hid. This is not a globally quiet-host benchmark. No samples were discarded. An immediately requested isolated Testbox was queued and stopped before dispatch, with no provider escalation. Production is x64, while this proof is ARM64; the synthetic parent also has fewer page-table bytes than the observed production process.

At 4 GiB, synchronous spawn accounts for 99% of the wall-time increase over the same small-memory process. Both Node 24 and Node 26 exhibit the cliff. Native CoW remains active; all 65,880 files and shared extents verify. Authority handshakes take about 0.1–0.2 seconds, not tens of seconds.

- **18 focused Linux owner/host tests pass under explicit Node 24.22.1 and pinned Bun 1.4.4** (Node 19.56 s Vitest / 28.07 s wrapper; Bun 5.46 s / 8.89 s). The strengthened 256-file regression fails on exact main `ecbad2ef` because two batches start two parent children instead of one; it passes on the fix.
- Real GNU cp held behind a FIFO proves silent authority revocation, cancellation, and unexpected helper exit cannot publish a batch or release staging before descendant pipes settle. Existing symlink/root replacement, occupied destination, exact timestamp, portable, and cross-filesystem contracts remain covered.
- Core and affected test typechecks pass. Both baseline and candidate Gateway builds pass. Full scoped `pnpm check:changed` completed; its own Promise-executor lint defect is repaired. The remaining 28 production / 8 full-tree unused-export signatures reproduce on exact original main parent `ecbad2ef`; new-to-this-lane owners are #196207 (`c7152f3b`), #192552 (`625945b7`), #196252 (`80ba593b`), and #191513 (`d85ebfe8`), with prior-lane attribution retained for the rest. These are reported main regressions, not ignored noise.
- Codex autoreview of the complete local candidate against `ecbad2ef`, P0–P2: **scoped-clean**, no actionable findings.
- Production **+167 LOC**, tests **+96 LOC**. Growth supplies the operation-owned helper lifecycle and the explicitly requested bounded diagnostics; the old per-batch large-parent spawn path is removed. Existing regression cases are strengthened/consolidated.

The actual built Gateway completed five serial interleaved pairs through `worktrees.create`, each with fresh state, an excluded cold `no-generation` warmup, and a measured warm btrfs `commit-changed` preparation. All 20 preparations verify all 65,880 selected payloads and the creation path-string ledger; all 20 remove RPC assertions pass.

| Pair | Baseline provisionCopy | Candidate provisionCopy | Baseline total preparation | Candidate total preparation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 47.040 s | 5.066 s | 68.102 s | 26.394 s |
| 2 | 59.246 s | 4.373 s | 84.553 s | 20.261 s |
| 3 | 61.146 s | 4.904 s | 79.190 s | 22.213 s |
| 4 | 62.140 s | 4.894 s | 76.815 s | 20.452 s |
| 5 | 69.580 s | 4.982 s | 84.291 s | 21.283 s |

**Gateway medians:** provisionCopy **61.146 → 4.904 s (12.47×)**; complete managed preparation **79.190 → 21.283 s**. Every measured candidate copy is 4.373–5.066 s. Excluded candidate cold warmups are 4.438–5.233 s. All candidate receipts report `linux-batched`, 515 batches, 1,647,000,000 logical bytes, one helper spawn, and 4,234 authority checks. The remaining preparation time is not represented as fixed.
 Initial CI found a Promise-executor lint error and missing Node MessagePort exception inventory entry; both are repaired. Bun also exposed FIFO fixture ordering, now repaired and green on both runtimes. Fresh Codex review of the repair is scoped-clean. The original base had 18 inherited test-line debt from #196680 (`3686da563`); integrating main `47b0ce478` resolves that named gate with 23 lines of slack. Its earlier inventory finding is fixed.

**Landing decision:** The lead explicitly accepted the completed fixture evidence and authorized landing, with exact-head CI green and ClawSweeper zero findings. No synthetic benchmark will run on the shared production host. After deployment, the first matching preparation's bounded `copyDetails` receipt will provide the serving-mount observation. The old receipt cannot establish the historical copier path retroactively, and these measurements do not claim an exact reproduction of its 74.2-second duration. No production deployment or restart is included.

## What Problem This Solves

Workspace preparation diagnostics lose the failing phase when a state-lease cancellation wraps the original error, and genuine lease-loss errors omit the next action.

## User Impact

Operators retain the actual failing preparation phase through causal wrappers. Genuine expired, replaced, or missing leases tell the caller to retry the operation. Caller access revocation remains a separate failure requiring access restoration.

## Why This Change Was Made

The timing owner matched errors by object identity even though the lease owner preserves the original failure as a cause. Reuse the existing error-graph traversal at both attribution points; unrelated later errors remain unattributed. Keep renewal scheduling, contention retries, expiry, transaction settlement, and closure-bound authority unchanged. No configuration or schema change.

Production code grows by five lines for the import and formatted comparisons; no new state or abstraction. Existing test fixtures gain 22 lines, with a scoped test-line allocation for wrapped/unrelated attribution and loss guidance. Related provisioning timing work in #193090 changes different logic in the same module.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes unbounded `scripts/pr` dependency-cache growth when operations are killed during installation or while retaining an anchor.

## User Impact

Subsequent PR commands automatically reclaim abandoned disposable cache state, with at most four cache/anchor directory removals per collection pass. Live operations and their children retain kernel-backed protection. No manual cache cleanup or configuration is needed.

Legacy holds without kernel evidence and unregistered directories use the approved scratch policy: older than 24 hours, with no current cwd, open descriptor or mapping reference. A dormant legacy child with only a pathname in memory can lose this disposable state and must reinstall on miss. New holds never fall back to age-based collection. Python 3 supplies the POSIX flock/census helper; children must preserve the inherited lifetime descriptor while using operation tooling.

## Why This Change Was Made

The lifetime owner previously relied on creator-driven anchor retirement and only collected ledger rows. SIGKILL left permanent holds; installation publication and eviction had filesystem/ledger windows that could leave invisible directories.

The owner now uses an inherited shared flock for future operations, requires a nonblocking exclusive flock for retirement, and records lifetime-creation and installation/detach intent before filesystem changes. Operations register immediately after acquiring the shared lock, including when installed dependencies avoid cache acquisition. Pending startup intent has no dependency consumers yet; recovery requires a dead creator incarnation, no current filesystem references, and an exclusive lock when its file exists. Node child-process APIs preserve the descriptor, including custom environments and execFile. Nested operations retain enclosing leases on additional descriptors while using their own FD7 lifetime. The collector removes dead anchors, settles abandoned installations, and handles legacy orphans under the metadata lock. Same-version additive tables record lifetime and transition evidence; the SQLite version is unchanged. Sealed device recovery includes that state and preserves exact replay and pre-lease v3 compatibility. Recovery commands do not run the startup sweep. Directory and file identity checks continue to refuse aliases.

Production/tooling growth is +1,443 net lines, counting scripts and generated code: 714 in the lifetime owner, 250 in the stdlib kernel/census helper, 168 in child-process inheritance, 31 in the wrapper, 11 in shared Python Git/publication launchers, 10 in their generated CI projection, six declarations and a 253-line synthetic benchmark. Runtime implementation growth is +1,174. This covers child-safe lifetime evidence, producer transitions, process census, bounded interrupted cleanup, nested runtime inheritance and sealed device recovery. Python launchers explicitly preserve declared lifetime descriptors; FD9 retirement authority is separate.

## Evidence

- Actual `scripts/pr` SIGKILL fixtures pass at installation, hold and settlement. Original orphan and install-wrapper regressions fail against exact parent `225afda642e9632775d7cfc520d1862736f50a19`.
- Enclosing-preload qualification: 200 tests across five affected files passed, with six existing platform skips. This includes the full wrapper suite, cache/materialized-anchor siblings and Node/Bun inheritance. Killing both outer and inner creators leaves a lazy grandchild protecting both lifetime locks.
- Collector suite: 14 passing cases, including bounded five-anchor shared-lease retirement and producer windows. Native census suite: 12 passing cases in both complete and restricted Linux procfs environments. Restricted hosts explicitly assert retention; inaccessible live processes never count as absent. A real unreadable zombie reproducer fails before the narrow fully-exited-group repair and passes afterward; a live unreadable reader remains protected.
- Device recovery: 18 focused cases pass, including pre-lease v3 ledgers with historical holds, pending file/stage/renamed states, sealed identities, refusal on aliases/replacements/changed rows and exact replay. The new-state regression fails before the recovery extension.
- Current-head CI exposed introduced Node-free and retained-projection recovery regressions; the startup collector now excludes recovery commands. Three minimal recovery cases pass locally. The three Linux retained-projection cases pass in CI run 42837213597. That run had one test-only failure: restricted census correctly retained an unsettled hold while the assertion expected settlement. The final head compares the full pre-sweep state, with actual-owner complete/restricted Linux proof and a separate clean Codex review. Final-head CI remains required.
- `pnpm check:changed` completed: all selected checks passed except the attributed inherited unused exports. Fresh Codex review of the final repair delta is scoped-clean through P2; the earlier complete patch was reviewed separately. Exact parent reproduces 28 production/eight full-tree unused-export failures, attributed to #192552, #196207, #196252, #191326, #191513, #190544 and #190205; these are main regressions, not ignored noise.
- Python boundary qualification: the full Git-owner and inheritance files pass under real primary/ancestor leases (100 passed, 20 existing platform skips). A persistent Node → Python owner → real Git → Node regression fails against the old owner and passes the fix. The Darwin native suite passes under the enclosing preload (31 cases, one existing skip); five affected Darwin census cases also pass. Canonical CI owner generation/check passes. Hosted review caught the original Python descriptor loss; the fix is in actual launch owners and fixture launch sites, with no copied-source workaround. Fresh Codex review of this delta is scoped-clean through P2.
- Synthetic Linux/btrfs fixture: 46 directories, 20 installations, 28 dead-creator holds, 26 orphans, 62,000 payload files / 1.18 GB. Two A/A controls and five fresh A/B pairs. Baseline retains 45 entries and all 28 holds; candidate reaches four entries and zero holds/anchors in 19 bounded calls. Allocated file blocks fall from 1.270 GB to 0.110 GB (1,159,307,264 allocated bytes reclaimed).
- Cleanup costs: final candidate total owner wall median/p95 1.716/1.882 seconds across 19 calls, per-call median/p95 77.9/170.0 ms. Baseline spends 43.6 ms median while leaving the leak. Whole-run process-tree CPU median is 1.168 seconds versus 0.290 seconds, including startup and fixture census/inventory but excluding setup. Warm empty owner calls increase from 1.05 to 16.96 ms; one-time additive adoption takes 69.34 ms. This is storage reclamation, not a latency improvement. The core owner revision was remeasured with five fresh candidate fixtures plus a baseline control after the original paired campaign. Later recovery-only changes are outside this benchmark path; shared-lease cleanup has separate paired proof (two-call wall median 366 ms before, 310 ms after, with the retained hold/anchor eliminated). Separate sampled owner allocations estimate 0.525 MB baseline versus 7.069 MB candidate (one diagnostic each; Python allocation excluded). Container-scale process census does not establish scan latency for thousands of host processes.

These are newly exposed main regressions requiring follow-up, not ignored noise. [ClawSweeper's published review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/196685#issuecomment-6769713685) names this exact head, has zero open checklist items and no actionable findings. issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Gateway shutdown can report `Plugin runtime still owns resources ... | service child cleanup identity lost: write EPIPE` when a service child exits while its stdin shutdown notification is being delivered.

## User Impact

Shutdown accepts completed child cleanup when the existing process owner verifies it. A missing closing receipt, lost lineage, or unverifiable process tree still fails cleanup. No configuration, schema, timeout, or public API changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stdin-end rejection permanently discarded cleanup authority before the closing receipt and native exit could settle. It now records the transport error and joins the existing bounded authority-close path. The same callback handles the existing control-stream and closing-acknowledgement errors; runtime production LOC is net zero.

The apparent plugin-close delay is separate: `plugin-registry` and `plugin-metadata` spans include process-supervisor and database closure. Disposal is already concurrent. Existing span evidence attributes 4,929ms of a 5,116ms metadata close to agent databases; no plugin scheduling change is justified. The database's internal wait remains unproven and is not fixed here.

## Evidence

- Initial exact-head CI run [42864521301](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42864521301) failed only the test-line ratchet and aggregate gate. Only outgoing stdin-end delivery is faulted; receipt, lineage EOF, and native process exit remain real.

Wrapper wall: 44.43s, mostly compilation; new native case: 287ms. The native file passed again after its lint correction (21.67s wrapper). The 87-line test allocation covers native boundary proof and the existing fixture's failure case.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes host disk and I/O stalls when an agent command crashes and inherits the Gateway’s unlimited core-size limit.

## User Impact

Linux agent commands and descendants receive a zero core-size limit, while the Gateway, spawn broker and internal workers retain their crash diagnostics. This covers ordinary and durable host commands, execa, PTYs and default Docker sandbox limits. Explicit sandbox `docker.ulimits.core` overrides remain supported.

Linux host execution requires util-linux `prlimit` in a trusted system directory (including the NixOS system profile). The kernel limit prevents direct-file cores; Linux pipe-based collectors apply their own policy. No host configuration or retention changes are made.

## Why This Change Was Made

Apply the existing agent execution intent before the dedicated command owner execs, with the same preparation for execa and PTY targets. `prlimit` execs in place and never changes the Gateway or broker limits. The dedicated anchor retains the target’s exact environment and custom `argv0`; the generic raw-spawn transport remains unchanged. Durable units receive `LimitCORE=0`, and the sandbox default participates in its existing reuse hash.

Production growth is 38 lines for the shared invocation preparation and owner wiring. No new configuration option, cache, schema or dependency package. The 106-line regression allocation covers a seeded positive parent limit, descendant inheritance, preserved internal limits/argv0, sandbox defaults/overrides the durable-unit contract, and NixOS binary resolution/missing dependency guidance.

## Evidence

- The seeded-limit regression is red on parent `ecbad2efa1d7e89d041965612b2237760a024c50` and green on the candidate. Agent root/descendant limits become `0/0`; parent/internal limits and custom target `argv0` remain intact.
- Linux Node 26.12.1, direct-file cores, five interleaved pairs plus A/A controls: agent SIGABRT cores fall from 339.64–339.90 MB (5/5) to zero (0/5); internal helper cores remain enabled. The 16-case transport matrix covers supervisor, execa, PTY and unchanged generic raw-spawn behavior.
- Real isolated Gateway startup (`/healthz` 200, startup settled) and SIGABRT control: Gateway and broker retain unlimited limits; the Gateway writes a complete 5,345,939,456-byte ELF core (exit 134, no OOM kill).
- Focused Node tests: 150 passes across the selected suites; the final PTY rerun also passed 15 tests and the NixOS correction passed 45 resolver/command tests, with platform skips recorded; pinned Bun sibling coverage also passes. The exact committed Linux regression callback and generated subprocess source are red on the parent and green on this head with a Node assertion adapter; the full Vitest runner is covered by the CI gate.
- `pnpm check:changed` completed. Task lint repairs pass focused checks; remaining failures are inherited dead exports (identical 28 production + 8 full-tree findings reproduced on the exact parent) and an 18-line test-budget debt introduced by #196680, subsequently reduced by #196636 and #196742. These are main regressions, not passing checks. Final Codex autoreview P0–P2 is scoped-clean after resolving its custom-argv0 finding by removing generic transport wrapping. Exact-head CI run 42869993764 succeeded. ClawSweeper reviewed final head `6ae775e8bcbe7` with zero findings and zero open checklist items.

| Owner metric, median | Parent | Final candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Healthy first launch | 141.545 ms | 140.054 ms |
| Healthy main-process CPU | 11.100 ms | 11.376 ms |
| Healthy main-isolate allocation | 4,871,920 B | 5,064,480 B |
| Crash completion | 163.415 ms | 121.065 ms |
| Crash main-process CPU | 5.308 ms | 3.927 ms |
| Crash main-isolate allocation | 3,867,600 B | 4,040,072 B |
| Agent crash core bytes | 339,763,200 B | 0 B |

Measurements are descriptive, not a latency or allocation improvement claim. Healthy A/A medians vary 197.236 / 145.703 ms, 14.549 / 12.655 ms CPU, and 5,038,240 / 4,665,944 B allocation. Final candidate crash allocation rises about 4.5%, and its maximum is 5,409,152 B versus 4,457,552 B baseline. Earlier runs remain in local evidence. CPU/allocation exclude subprocesses.

Reproduction is in `scripts/perf/agent-core-dump-proof.mts`. It uses a 16 MiB synthetic child payload on Linux ARM64/overlayfs. This owner does not read the agent database or workspace inventory; large-database/btrfs fleet scale is not claimed. Live durable user-manager proof was setup-blocked by the disposable image’s missing PAM module; its unit-property regression passes.

Inherited dead-export attribution: identical 28 production + 8 full-tree findings on the exact parent. Source cutovers/exports introduced by #196207, #192552, #196252, #191326, #139911, #190205, #132716, #129184, #190544, #191513 and commit `a7436c8b4a93bff59d099661d2b206bb0627ac2b`. No ignores or unrelated exports were changed to hide these main regressions.

Hosted review found that a fixed `/usr/bin/prlimit` path breaks NixOS. The correction reuses the existing trusted-system-binary resolver and reports how to install util-linux if absent. A disposable Linux fixture with prlimit only under `/run/current-system/sw/bin` fails with ENOENT on the first PR head and passes on the correction; candidate agent SIGABRT writes zero core bytes and internal-helper SIGABRT writes 339,636,224 bytes.

The first corrected head exposed an extraction-inventory omission in CI: the trusted PR wrapper and copied provisioning fixtures could not load the new helper. The final correction adds `src/process/linux-core-dump.ts` and `src/infra/resolve-system-bin.ts` to `scripts/pr-lib/wrapper-components.txt`. The three failing source/import closure assertions reproduce red before the two-line fix and pass afterward. The local provisioning replay passed 16 cases and skipped one Linux-only case. Its additional Darwin cold/warm/sparse testcase exceeded the existing 120-second timeout on both this branch (212.84 seconds) and exact main parent `ecbad2efa1d7e89d041965612b2237760a024c50` under matching Node 26.12.1 (204.777 seconds). The 120-second default originates in #118042 and the unchanged six-call workload in #149585; the first historical performance threshold crossing was not bisected. The timeout remains recorded as a main-local failure; it was not increased or suppressed. Final-head remote CI passed. Runtime source and the Linux crash measurements are unchanged by this inventory correction.

Fixes full-history downloads when an agent runs a Git content command naming a commit missing from a shared blobless clone, even when the clone already contains almost all of that history.

## User Impact

Commands such as `git show <commit>:path`, revision diffs, log, restore, checkout, and merge-base fetch missing commits with history negotiation before reading content. Existing offline probes remain offline. If origin cannot supply an object, the command stops with guidance to fetch from its owning remote rather than retrying through Git's expensive lazy-fetch path.

The common present-commit path adds one offline batched object check and no network traffic. Measured Linux overhead is about 1.4 ms per command; macOS adds about 11.5 ms on the measured host. No configuration or migration is required. Absolute Git paths, aliases, and revisions supplied on stdin remain outside this preparation path.

Git's [promisor fetch implementation](https://github.com/git/git/blob/v2.56.0/promisor-remote.c#L43-L46) forces noop negotiation, so repository configuration cannot make lazy fetches send local haves. Related: #196662

**Maintainer decision: land on the counterbalanced pilot evidence. Final measurement acceptance remains pending because shared-host contention and unstable A/A controls prevented a qualified full campaign.**

## What Problem This Solves

Taking and recursively removing a full btrfs snapshot on every changed command reduced container pauses but added 28% command latency and CPU in the original 62,000-file benchmark. Small workspaces should not pay that snapshot cost.

## User Impact

Small, fast checkpoints keep direct paused capture. Expensive checkpoints retain atomic capture and resume before scanning. Commands still wait for canonical acceptance; after runtime resume, the workspace lease renames the disposable capture to a unique retired path and hands cleanup to the existing run-end lifetime. The next command can execute during deletion; the next snapshot waits for pending cleanup and retries interrupted removals before creating another artifact.

Cleanup keeps the existing native recursive remover and needs no new utility, privilege or mount option. Snapshot creation can still wait for dirty writeback, and nested subvolumes retain the complete paused fallback.

## Why This Change Was Made

The manifest worker already knows the accepted entry count. It now carries that fact on an early-aborting probe, so a large tree is recognized even when the changed pathname sorts first. A 20,000-entry inventory or a probe lasting 500 ms selects snapshots. No additional scan, persistent cache, schema, or configuration is introduced. Recovery and initial layout capture without probe facts remain on the direct path.

Canonical writes retain session authority. The lease transfers only an immutable, disposable artifact to independent cleanup. Unique retired names prevent delayed deletion from touching a later capture. Pending promises track active work, not cached scan results; persistent removal failures prevent another snapshot from growing the backlog. A rolling snapshot cannot be refreshed by the current immutable-copy primitive, and an early probe is not a complete changed-path set for safe selective reflinks.

The snapshot manifest scan also avoids one asynchronous filesystem dispatch per metadata read inside the existing capture worker. A shared 32-read yield services cancellation; the main thread and non-snapshot scans retain asynchronous reads. File hashing, identity and containment checks are unchanged.

## Evidence

Two regressions fail on the parent: small btrfs checkpoints unnecessarily invoke snapshots, and completed commands remain blocked behind capture deletion. On the candidate all 9 checkpoint scenarios pass, including interrupted acceptance, nested fallback, later guest writes, canonical read-after-command, bounded cleanup custody and caller disposal. Native filesystem owner tests: 10/10. The broader projection owner run passed 83 tests with 2 platform skips; its one obsolete always-snapshot recovery expectation was corrected and replayed green.

The next-command overlap regressions additionally fail on preliminary head a04f5a346a0db94ff634fc0d5969edee4e729ba3 with `OPENCLAW_STATE_LEASE_HELD`, then pass on the retired-path handoff. Final staged candidate Codex autoreview is scoped-clean through P2. Production delta: +125 LOC: 103 for adaptive capture and bounded lifetime transfer/recovery, plus 22 for worker metadata reads. Tests: +205 LOC, including real-worker scan equivalence and cooperative cancellation; the two scanner/worker test files pass all 45 tests. The checkpoint test registrations move to their existing fixture module to stay within the file limit without dropping coverage.

`pnpm check:changed --base 4ec97ef5e73e0780cb0d9a70d096a1bba5600027` completed on the final candidate: all categories pass except the inherited unused-export scans. Both reproduce on the exact parent with identical 28/8 symbol sets and attributed introducing commits. These are existing main regressions. The runtime build also passes. The nine checkpoint cases take 57.24 s including cold compilation (54.17 s Vitest duration, 63% transform and 35% tests); they exercise the actual SQLite lease and lifecycle boundary. The maintainer explicitly accepted the pilot for landing; the incomplete final native campaign remains a measurement limitation, not completed proof.

The exact 205 regression lines have a justified allocation record, and the test-line guard passes against the branch parent. Final-head CI run `42859153410` passes every job except baseline-ratchets and its dependent CI gate. The exact CI main parent `ecbad2efa1d7e89d041965612b2237760a024c50` independently reproduces 18 lines of debt: 6,632,310 test lines against a 6,632,292 ceiling. #196680 (`3686da563c54738b11fac5c9a103ee8b3943b5e6`) introduced 21 lines of debt; #196636 and #196742 paid down three. This PR adds 205 test lines and 205 credit, leaving the inherited debt unchanged. This remains a named main regression.

Final-head CodeQL and OpenGrep initially completed analysis but failed while uploading SARIF because of GitHub installation API rate limits. Only those failed jobs were rerun after diagnosis; both workflows succeeded on attempt 2. No security exception or alert dismissal was used. ClawSweeper reviewed the final source head and reports zero findings.

### Native measurement acceptance, recorded before the campaign

Final performance results are pending. The first complete adaptive/cleanup campaign passed small-workspace latency and large pause goals, but did not establish a CPU improvement over the snapshot-every-command implementation, so it was held. A counterbalanced 20-command metadata pilot reduced command median from 2623 to 2088 ms and cgroup CPU from 4694 to 3346 ms/command; snapshot scan time fell from 1517 to 999 ms. All read checks passed. These are pilot results, not the final acceptance campaign.

The first final-head small campaign was affected by another benchmark becoming active in the shared Docker VM. All consistency checks passed, but the whole attempt is retained as contended evidence, not performance acceptance. Subsequent quiet 10/10 controls still differed by 24.7% in command median, despite only 4.6% CPU variation. Recorded phases place most variation in command/engine control and staging waits; manifest scan stayed at 23 ms. Those controls are retained. One explicitly recorded small-workspace protocol revision uses the unchanged driver with 10 warmup and 50 measured commands per arm (`--requests 5`), improving sample resolution without assuming a warmup cause. The large protocol stays 10/10; outcome targets are unchanged. The revised first control passed correctness but failed its independent resource gate: another workload consumed 34.43 CPU-seconds and 563.85 MB reads during 60.22 seconds. No second control or paired campaign followed. All native timing is now idle pending a reserved quiet interval; no favorable subset or repeated-until-green controls will be selected.

The selected runtime and extended worker-allocation driver are pinned to `12227a56a740261516bb036efcad77fa8078837f`. Fresh full-candidate Codex autoreview is scoped-clean through P2; runtime build, targeted checks and the 205-line test allocation pass. The maintainer accepted the pilot for landing at this exact head under the review/security gates and the documented inherited-CI exception. Pilot command median 2.09 s is below the earlier pre-#196662 baseline of 2.37 s, but that comparison is across campaigns, not a qualified final paired comparison. Pilot pause p95 is 223 ms, cgroup CPU improves 28.7%, and all consistency checks pass. Shared-host noise leaves final two-regime acceptance, worker allocation and writeback diagnostics pending. The committed driver is `scripts/perf/local-workspace-checkpoint-measure.ts`; writeback diagnostics use `scripts/perf/local-workspace-snapshot-writeback.py`.

Use real Podman+btrfs, 62,000 files/1.1 GB and 100 files/400 KiB, with the same approximately 35 GiB synthetic agent database and 10,000 sessions. Compare pre-#196662 source 3f17d921f6cc1cf03d52054a74ba3a5e885f5c35, shipped 10d67445fbecbc3c25f9bb5a5020766e3513b64b, and this pinned candidate. Each large formal arm has 10 warm-up and 10 measured mutating commands; the revised small arms have 10 warm-up and 50 measured commands, with canonical and next-guest read checks throughout. Run A/A controls and five counterbalanced baseline/candidate pairs per regime; retain slow and failed arms.

Small-workspace command median must match or improve the pre-change baseline within measured A/A spread, with zero snapshots. Large-workspace pause p95 must be at most 300 ms, with command latency and total CPU materially below the snapshot-every-command implementation. Report remaining differences from the pre-change baseline explicitly. No 20% latency/CPU regression is accepted implicitly.

Include the final cleanup tail outside per-command latency but inside burst CPU/wall accounting. Wait for btrfs kernel deletion work and report whole-VM CPU as well as cgroup CPU, since kernel cleaner work can escape container accounting. Measure allocation separately and keep instrumented profiles out of plain latency results. Dirty-writeback tests compare source churn at 1.7 GB/hour, explicit pre-syncfs, and separately labeled 1.1 GB bursts; they cannot retrospectively attribute an untraced historical pause.

ClawSweeper gate: address every open item by number and obtain zero open items on the final head before merge.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes unbounded `scripts/pr` dependency-cache growth when operations are killed during installation or while retaining an anchor.

## User Impact

Subsequent PR commands automatically reclaim abandoned disposable cache state, with at most four cache/anchor directory removals per collection pass. Live operations and their children retain kernel-backed protection. No manual cache cleanup or configuration is needed.

Legacy holds without kernel evidence and unregistered directories use the approved scratch policy: older than 24 hours, with no current cwd, open descriptor or mapping reference. A dormant legacy child with only a pathname in memory can lose this disposable state and must reinstall on miss. New holds never fall back to age-based collection. Python 3 supplies the POSIX flock/census helper; children must preserve the inherited lifetime descriptor while using operation tooling.

## Why This Change Was Made

The lifetime owner previously relied on creator-driven anchor retirement and only collected ledger rows. SIGKILL left permanent holds; installation publication and eviction had filesystem/ledger windows that could leave invisible directories.

The owner now uses an inherited shared flock for future operations, requires a nonblocking exclusive flock for retirement, and records lifetime-creation and installation/detach intent before filesystem changes. Operations register immediately after acquiring the shared lock, including when installed dependencies avoid cache acquisition. Pending startup intent has no dependency consumers yet; recovery requires a dead creator incarnation, no current filesystem references, and an exclusive lock when its file exists. Node child-process APIs preserve the descriptor, including custom environments and execFile. Nested operations retain enclosing leases on additional descriptors while using their own FD7 lifetime. The collector removes dead anchors, settles abandoned installations, and handles legacy orphans under the metadata lock. Same-version additive tables record lifetime and transition evidence; the SQLite version is unchanged. Sealed device recovery includes that state and preserves exact replay and pre-lease v3 compatibility. Recovery commands do not run the startup sweep. Directory and file identity checks continue to refuse aliases.

Production/tooling growth is +1,443 net lines, counting scripts and generated code: 714 in the lifetime owner, 250 in the stdlib kernel/census helper, 168 in child-process inheritance, 31 in the wrapper, 11 in shared Python Git/publication launchers, 10 in their generated CI projection, six declarations and a 253-line synthetic benchmark. Runtime implementation growth is +1,174. This covers child-safe lifetime evidence, producer transitions, process census, bounded interrupted cleanup, nested runtime inheritance and sealed device recovery. Python launchers explicitly preserve declared lifetime descriptors; FD9 retirement authority is separate.

## Evidence

- Actual `scripts/pr` SIGKILL fixtures pass at installation, hold and settlement. Original orphan and install-wrapper regressions fail against exact parent `225afda642e9632775d7cfc520d1862736f50a19`.
- Enclosing-preload qualification: 200 tests across five affected files passed, with six existing platform skips. This includes the full wrapper suite, cache/materialized-anchor siblings and Node/Bun inheritance. Killing both outer and inner creators leaves a lazy grandchild protecting both lifetime locks.
- Collector suite: 14 passing cases, including bounded five-anchor shared-lease retirement and producer windows. Native census suite: 12 passing cases in both complete and restricted Linux procfs environments. Restricted hosts explicitly assert retention; inaccessible live processes never count as absent. A real unreadable zombie reproducer fails before the narrow fully-exited-group repair and passes afterward; a live unreadable reader remains protected.
- Device recovery: 18 focused cases pass, including pre-lease v3 ledgers with historical holds, pending file/stage/renamed states, sealed identities, refusal on aliases/replacements/changed rows and exact replay. The new-state regression fails before the recovery extension.
- Current-head CI exposed introduced Node-free and retained-projection recovery regressions; the startup collector now excludes recovery commands. Three minimal recovery cases pass locally. The three Linux retained-projection cases pass in CI run 42837213597. That run had one test-only failure: restricted census correctly retained an unsettled hold while the assertion expected settlement. The final head compares the full pre-sweep state, with actual-owner complete/restricted Linux proof and a separate clean Codex review. Final-head CI remains required.
- `pnpm check:changed` completed: all selected checks passed except the attributed inherited unused exports. Fresh Codex review of the final repair delta is scoped-clean through P2; the earlier complete patch was reviewed separately. Exact parent reproduces 28 production/eight full-tree unused-export failures, attributed to #192552, #196207, #196252, #191326, #191513, #190544 and #190205; these are main regressions, not ignored noise.
- Python boundary qualification: the full Git-owner and inheritance files pass under real primary/ancestor leases (100 passed, 20 existing platform skips). A persistent Node → Python owner → real Git → Node regression fails against the old owner and passes the fix. The Darwin native suite passes under the enclosing preload (31 cases, one existing skip); five affected Darwin census cases also pass. Canonical CI owner generation/check passes. Hosted review caught the original Python descriptor loss; the fix is in actual launch owners and fixture launch sites, with no copied-source workaround. Fresh Codex review of this delta is scoped-clean through P2.
- Synthetic Linux/btrfs fixture: 46 directories, 20 installations, 28 dead-creator holds, 26 orphans, 62,000 payload files / 1.18 GB. Two A/A controls and five fresh A/B pairs. Baseline retains 45 entries and all 28 holds; candidate reaches four entries and zero holds/anchors in 19 bounded calls. Allocated file blocks fall from 1.270 GB to 0.110 GB (1,159,307,264 allocated bytes reclaimed).
- Cleanup costs: final candidate total owner wall median/p95 1.716/1.882 seconds across 19 calls, per-call median/p95 77.9/170.0 ms. Baseline spends 43.6 ms median while leaving the leak. Whole-run process-tree CPU median is 1.168 seconds versus 0.290 seconds, including startup and fixture census/inventory but excluding setup. Warm empty owner calls increase from 1.05 to 16.96 ms; one-time additive adoption takes 69.34 ms. This is storage reclamation, not a latency improvement. The core owner revision was remeasured with five fresh candidate fixtures plus a baseline control after the original paired campaign. Later recovery-only changes are outside this benchmark path; shared-lease cleanup has separate paired proof (two-call wall median 366 ms before, 310 ms after, with the retained hold/anchor eliminated). Separate sampled owner allocations estimate 0.525 MB baseline versus 7.069 MB candidate (one diagnostic each; Python allocation excluded). Container-scale process census does not establish scan latency for thousands of host processes.

Only synthetic disposable fixtures were used; no production cache or data was accessed. No Control UI imports are affected. Final-head CI and ClawSweeper review remain required before landing.
## Final landing evidence

Reviewed head: `6b9712fd3435a4f27004a4be6eccc63c8f0e9fd8`. [CI run 42849960561](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42849960561), attempt 1, tested merge `ff9a8491578f4d7ece62748c3a0bafb66931d288` against exact main parent `d5a021ebabecfdada396c9ac1567e3bbdf04be0a`. Every selected job passes except the three proven inherited failures below and their aggregate gate. Security-fast, all seven Security High jobs and precise scanning pass. Failed CI remains failed; the authorized native inherited-failure admission is being used.

- **Test budget (#196680, `3686da563c54738b11fac5c9a103ee8b3943b5e6`):** the introducer's exact parent passes with seven lines of credit; the merge adds 28 lines without credit. Exact final CI main parent reproduces the resulting 21-line deficit (6,629,462 lines / 6,629,441 ceiling). Both intervening commits fully cover their additions. This PR allocates exactly its own 1,152-line growth.
- **QA profiles 2/4 and 4/4 (#196570, `e230abd098ed970c30a9812813d2a77b5e80640a`):** both real mock-provider scenarios reproduce on that exact main parent, each timing out after 60 seconds with the same event sequence and closed plugin invocation scope during completion delivery. An unchanged actual-owner fixture using the real plugin instance, registry and prepared model lease succeeds on immediate parent `685f18a41b28b07e93b411b895be1c60dec3fc23` and fails at the introducing commit. Ordinary channel calls still work; the delayed callback alone inherits a disposed turn scope. All seven named scenario/owner inputs are byte-identical between the tested main parent and PR merge.

These are newly exposed main regressions requiring follow-up, not ignored noise. Exact-parent command logs, scenario results, adjacent-commit observations and source identities are retained by the native admission evidence. The previously documented local unused-export regressions remain separately attributed.

[ClawSweeper's published review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/196685#issuecomment-6769713685) names this exact head, has zero open checklist items and no actionable findings. All nine earlier items and both hosted Codex findings are reconciled in [one numbered response](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/196685#issuecomment-6770742298). The review's then-pending smoke attribution is completed above. Both hosted discussion threads are resolved.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Changed sandbox commands freeze the guest throughout workspace discovery, Git capture, and canonical reconciliation. With large workspaces, scanning alone can take seconds while every process in the container is paused.

## User Impact

For provisioned btrfs subvolumes, checkpoint now pauses for the existing native snapshot operation, resumes the guest, and synchronizes canonical state from that captured tree. Command completion still waits for canonical acceptance, preserving read-after-command consistency. Initial recovery and imports retain their existing pause boundaries. No configuration, schema, dependency, or cache is added.

## Why This Change Was Made

The checkpoint owner reuses the template backend's native copy primitive under its existing lease. Snapshot fingerprints translate only the proven snapshot device back to the source identity, preserving unchanged probes. Btrfs omits nested subvolumes: the manifest walker detects its inode-2 placeholders before accepting a receipt, then re-pauses under the same lease and uses the existing complete Git capture. Unsupported backends and ordinary directories also retain that path, resuming after durable capture.

The owner removes its private capture after resume and removes leftovers on the next lease. Native removal now repairs inaccessible directories only after a permission failure; it does not follow symlinks or change live source permissions. This is required for snapshots containing ordinary read-only workspace directories.

Snapshot creation can wait for btrfs dirty-data writeback, so this bounds the paused work rather than promising a fixed wall-clock limit. Recursive snapshot cleanup adds work after resume; the native comparison will report that cost explicitly.

## Evidence

The real Podman+btrfs comparison completed all five counterbalanced pairs: 50 measured mutating commands per arm, plus two A/A controls. Every command passed canonical and subsequent guest read checks. The fixture contains 62,000 synthetic files / 1.1 GB, 10,001 session metadata rows, and a 33.65 GiB synthetic database. No production data was used.

| Metric | Parent | Atomic capture |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Pause p50 / p95 / max | 1,619.63 / 1,830.52 / 4,497.19 ms | 194.23 / 241.48 / 269.72 ms |
| Command p50 / p95 / max | 2,374.14 / 2,854.99 / 7,252.07 ms | 3,038.07 / 3,665.20 / 4,221.59 ms |
| Whole-cgroup CPU per command | 3,493.06 ms | 4,472.75 ms |
| Main-isolate allocation per command | 19.22 MB | 20.49 MB |

Median pause improves 88%; median command latency and whole-cgroup CPU increase 28%. A/A pause, command and CPU spread was about 1–1.3%; allocation spread was 9.4%, so no allocation benefit is claimed. All pairs, including the slower first candidate arm, are retained. The 1.36–1.42 s manifest scan runs paused on the parent and unpaused on the candidate in all 50 commands. Native snapshot copy takes 106 ms median; recursive cleanup takes 511 ms after resume. Cleanup explains most of the extra command latency. The maximum guest heartbeat gap falls from 4.43 s to 243 ms.

Timing uses parent `3f17d921f6cc1cf03d52054a74ba3a5e885f5c35` and implementation `64147937916763407221bef031a138af43dd40a8`, with the same frozen harness. Final head `32b8f86f7fc49989f7ae6ab5c1346831b82b5be6` changes only type placement and emits byte-identical JavaScript. The harness runs on a task-owned Linux ARM64 rig with four CPUs and 12 GiB memory, Podman 4.3.1, btrfs 6.2, and Node 26.12.1 for allocation accounting. CPU includes native helpers, Git and the guest; allocation covers only the main V8 isolate. Separate baseline/candidate profiles passed and are excluded from these timing distributions. Final-head native nested-subvolume fallback also passed: two pauses of 180.84 and 5,387.44 ms, complete nested canonical contents, correct next guest read, preserved 0555 source permissions, and no capture artifact. The matching baseline paused 5,947.87 ms; both perform full hashing because the existing fingerprint format rejects mixed-device reuse. This single diagnostic pair is excluded from performance statistics and is not a timing-improvement claim. An oversized 20-command functional run hit its 240-second deadline after at least 17 completed commands; that partial run is retained, and the bounded follow-up changed only the proof driver loop count to one.

- Atomic ordering regressions fail on the prior head because manifest scanning still observes a paused guest. Final affected replay: 17 passed, including seven authority-loss cases. Broader touched-owner proof before the operation-file extraction: 125 passed, two existing platform skips.
- Read-only artifact removal regression fails before the fix with EACCES; all ten native-owner tests now pass. Real Linux btrfs create/copy/remove also passes as UID 501 with no effective capabilities, preserving live nested contents and read-only modes.
- Final `pnpm check:changed --base 3f17d921f6cc1cf03d52054a74ba3a5e885f5c35`: all categories pass except the exact inherited unused-export set below. These are existing main regressions, not passing checks.
- Independent Codex review of the final atomic implementation: scoped-clean through P2, with final source-integrity verification. Prior-head green CI and hosted reviews do not cover this revision; fresh exact-head checks remain required.

Production delta: +199 lines, including snapshot lifecycle/cleanup, nested-subvolume fallback, and source identity preservation. Moving the existing projection operation whole keeps one lifecycle owner within the line cap. Test delta: +245 lines for ordering, recovery, fingerprint reuse, fallback, authority loss, and artifact permissions. Benchmark code is proof-only.

CI on `64147937916763407221bef031a138af43dd40a8` found one introduced static type-import cycle. The repair moves the capture contract into the existing workspace types module and imports it directly. The exact failing guard is red on that head and green after repair; targeted typechecking passes. All six changed files emit byte-identical JavaScript, so the native comparison remains runtime-equivalent. The repair is committed as `32b8f86f7fc49989f7ae6ab5c1346831b82b5be6` and passes fresh Codex review. No admin exception or CI rerun was needed.

Both Knip scans exit 1 on parent `3f17d921f6cc1cf03d52054a74ba3a5e885f5c35`; normalized symbol sets match the final candidate check exactly, with no module-resolution failures. Owner history and consumer-removal patches identify these sources:

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes full-history downloads when an agent runs a Git content command naming a commit missing from a shared blobless clone, even when the clone already contains almost all of that history.

## User Impact

Commands such as `git show <commit>:path`, revision diffs, log, restore, checkout, and merge-base fetch missing commits with history negotiation before reading content. Existing offline probes remain offline. If origin cannot supply an object, the command stops with guidance to fetch from its owning remote rather than retrying through Git's expensive lazy-fetch path.

The common present-commit path adds one offline batched object check and no network traffic. Measured Linux overhead is about 1.4 ms per command; macOS adds about 11.5 ms on the measured host. No configuration or migration is required. Absolute Git paths, aliases, and revisions supplied on stdin remain outside this preparation path.

## Why This Change Was Made

Git's [promisor fetch implementation](https://github.com/git/git/blob/v2.56.0/promisor-remote.c#L43-L46) forces noop negotiation, so repository configuration cannot make lazy fetches send local haves. Refreshing selected heads cannot cover arbitrary commit IDs. The existing agent Git shim now prepares revision roots at the command boundary, preserving Git's global options, normal content hydration, refs, and FETCH_HEAD. Unknown names and non-revision arguments remain Git's responsibility.

Runtime production growth is 93 lines for revision preparation and the missing-object fetch path. The existing global-option/query owner is reused; no cache, new dependency, or parallel fetch owner was introduced. The simplification pass removed unnecessary shell forks and duplicate shared-worktree detection. A scoped 138-line test allocation covers the real native-Git regression and argument/negative cases, including staged restore flags and path-only `diff --no-index`.

## Evidence

Synthetic blobless clone with 126,357 commits and 884,499 trees: clone shallow, explicitly unshallow, create linked worktree, advance origin by one commit, then run the actual shim's `show <missing>:path`. Five counterbalanced A/B and five A/A samples; final shell simplifications replayed candidate measurements against the unchanged graph.

| Missing-command metric | Before median / p95 | After median / p95 |

| Received objects | 1,010,865 / 1,010,865 | 9 / 9 |
| Received pack bytes | 54,880,025 / 54,880,025 | 531 / 531 |
| Wall ms | 6,100.854 / 6,172.292 | 156.010 / 205.300 |
| Native CPU ms | 6,460 / 6,480 | 50 / 50 |
| Peak RSS MB | 397.72 / 399.08 | 9.85 / 9.90 |

A/A wall drift: 3.2%. Linux present-command median/p95: 1.895/1.984 → 3.294/3.690 ms, CPU 1.5 → 3 ms, unchanged median RSS, zero fetched objects. Linux A/A drift −1.2%. macOS present median: 16.927 → 28.438 ms. CPU includes the local upload-pack server; RSS is not cumulative allocation, which was not measured. This native shell/Git path has no JavaScript allocation. Local file transport/APFS and Linux container controls do not claim production network/btrfs latency or simulate unrelated application databases.

Reproduce with `python3 scripts/perf/pr-worktree-fetch.py <new-proof-directory> --pairs 5 --aa-pairs 5 --baseline-shim <exported-base-shim> --candidate-shim <exported-candidate-shim>`; the same committed workload has fixture-reuse and present-only modes.

The native regression fails on base because `show` retransfers existing history (17 objects versus a four-object bound). Owner suite: 2/2 tests passed, including the native command table (5.706s) and existing exec integration (8.551s); wrapper 54.74s including cold compilation. The final argument follow-up reran the expanded native table successfully (5.588s; wrapper43.31s); both new cases were red before their fixes. Final infra typecheck, scoped format/lint, and diff checks pass. Codex P0–P2 autoreview is scoped-clean for the complete candidate against `ac7e941722ab32fcf019ef257fc52819fa71da07` and the subsequent argument-only delta against `940e263fb77ed78b3dfd35a284596e5bb94f00d6`. issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes unbounded `scripts/pr` dependency-cache growth when operations are killed during installation or while retaining an anchor.

## User Impact

Subsequent PR commands automatically reclaim abandoned disposable cache state, with at most four cache/anchor directory removals per collection pass. Live operations and their children retain kernel-backed protection. No manual cache cleanup or configuration is needed.

Legacy holds without kernel evidence and unregistered directories use the approved scratch policy: older than 24 hours, with no current cwd, open descriptor or mapping reference. A dormant legacy child with only a pathname in memory can lose this disposable state and must reinstall on miss. New holds never fall back to age-based collection. Python 3 supplies the POSIX flock/census helper; children must preserve the inherited lifetime descriptor while using operation tooling.

## Why This Change Was Made

The lifetime owner previously relied on creator-driven anchor retirement and only collected ledger rows. SIGKILL left permanent holds; installation publication and eviction had filesystem/ledger windows that could leave invisible directories.

The owner now uses an inherited shared flock for future operations, requires a nonblocking exclusive flock for retirement, and records lifetime-creation and installation/detach intent before filesystem changes. Operations register immediately after acquiring the shared lock, including when installed dependencies avoid cache acquisition. Pending startup intent has no dependency consumers yet; recovery requires a dead creator incarnation, no current filesystem references, and an exclusive lock when its file exists. Node child-process APIs preserve the descriptor, including custom environments and execFile. Nested operations retain enclosing leases on additional descriptors while using their own FD7 lifetime. The collector removes dead anchors, settles abandoned installations, and handles legacy orphans under the metadata lock. Same-version additive tables record lifetime and transition evidence; the SQLite version is unchanged. Sealed device recovery includes that state and preserves exact replay and pre-lease v3 compatibility. Recovery commands do not run the startup sweep. Directory and file identity checks continue to refuse aliases.

Production/tooling growth is +1,443 net lines, counting scripts and generated code: 714 in the lifetime owner, 250 in the stdlib kernel/census helper, 168 in child-process inheritance, 31 in the wrapper, 11 in shared Python Git/publication launchers, 10 in their generated CI projection, six declarations and a 253-line synthetic benchmark. Runtime implementation growth is +1,174. This covers child-safe lifetime evidence, producer transitions, process census, bounded interrupted cleanup, nested runtime inheritance and sealed device recovery. Python launchers explicitly preserve declared lifetime descriptors; FD9 retirement authority is separate.

## Evidence

- Actual `scripts/pr` SIGKILL fixtures pass at installation, hold and settlement. Original orphan and install-wrapper regressions fail against exact parent `225afda642e9632775d7cfc520d1862736f50a19`.
- Enclosing-preload qualification: 200 tests across five affected files passed, with six existing platform skips. This includes the full wrapper suite, cache/materialized-anchor siblings and Node/Bun inheritance. Killing both outer and inner creators leaves a lazy grandchild protecting both lifetime locks.
- Collector suite: 14 passing cases, including bounded five-anchor shared-lease retirement and producer windows. Native census suite: 12 passing cases in both complete and restricted Linux procfs environments. Restricted hosts explicitly assert retention; inaccessible live processes never count as absent. A real unreadable zombie reproducer fails before the narrow fully-exited-group repair and passes afterward; a live unreadable reader remains protected.
- Device recovery: 18 focused cases pass, including pre-lease v3 ledgers with historical holds, pending file/stage/renamed states, sealed identities, refusal on aliases/replacements/changed rows and exact replay. The new-state regression fails before the recovery extension.
- Current-head CI exposed introduced Node-free and retained-projection recovery regressions; the startup collector now excludes recovery commands. Three minimal recovery cases pass locally. The three Linux retained-projection cases pass in CI run 42837213597. That run had one test-only failure: restricted census correctly retained an unsettled hold while the assertion expected settlement. The final head compares the full pre-sweep state, with actual-owner complete/restricted Linux proof and a separate clean Codex review. Final-head CI remains required.
- `pnpm check:changed` completed: all selected checks passed except the attributed inherited unused exports. Fresh Codex review of the final repair delta is scoped-clean through P2; the earlier complete patch was reviewed separately. Exact parent reproduces 28 production/eight full-tree unused-export failures, attributed to #192552, #196207, #196252, #191326, #191513, #190544 and #190205; these are main regressions, not ignored noise.
- Python boundary qualification: the full Git-owner and inheritance files pass under real primary/ancestor leases (100 passed, 20 existing platform skips). A persistent Node → Python owner → real Git → Node regression fails against the old owner and passes the fix. The Darwin native suite passes under the enclosing preload (31 cases, one existing skip); five affected Darwin census cases also pass. Canonical CI owner generation/check passes. Hosted review caught the original Python descriptor loss; the fix is in actual launch owners and fixture launch sites, with no copied-source workaround. Fresh Codex review of this delta is scoped-clean through P2.
- Synthetic Linux/btrfs fixture: 46 directories, 20 installations, 28 dead-creator holds, 26 orphans, 62,000 payload files / 1.18 GB. Two A/A controls and five fresh A/B pairs. Baseline retains 45 entries and all 28 holds; candidate reaches four entries and zero holds/anchors in 19 bounded calls. Allocated file blocks fall from 1.270 GB to 0.110 GB (1,159,307,264 allocated bytes reclaimed).
- Cleanup costs: final candidate total owner wall median/p95 1.716/1.882 seconds across 19 calls, per-call median/p95 77.9/170.0 ms. Baseline spends 43.6 ms median while leaving the leak. Whole-run process-tree CPU median is 1.168 seconds versus 0.290 seconds, including startup and fixture census/inventory but excluding setup. Warm empty owner calls increase from 1.05 to 16.96 ms; one-time additive adoption takes 69.34 ms. This is storage reclamation, not a latency improvement. The core owner revision was remeasured with five fresh candidate fixtures plus a baseline control after the original paired campaign. Later recovery-only changes are outside this benchmark path; shared-lease cleanup has separate paired proof (two-call wall median 366 ms before, 310 ms after, with the retained hold/anchor eliminated). Separate sampled owner allocations estimate 0.525 MB baseline versus 7.069 MB candidate (one diagnostic each; Python allocation excluded). Container-scale process census does not establish scan latency for thousands of host processes.

Only synthetic disposable fixtures were used; no production cache or data was accessed. No Control UI imports are affected. Final-head CI and ClawSweeper review remain required before landing.
## Final landing evidence

Reviewed head: `6b9712fd3435a4f27004a4be6eccc63c8f0e9fd8`. Ordinary channel calls still work; the delayed callback alone inherits a disposed turn scope. All seven named scenario/owner inputs are byte-identical between the tested main parent and PR merge.

These are newly exposed main regressions requiring follow-up, not ignored noise. Exact-parent command logs, scenario results, adjacent-commit observations and source identities are retained by the native admission evidence. The previously documented local unused-export regressions remain separately attributed.

[ClawSweeper's published review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/196685#issuecomment-6769713685) names this exact head, has zero open checklist items and no actionable findings. ## What Problem This Solves

Fast scrolling can present an almost empty transcript while the newly admitted rows are being measured and painted. The range policy drops the preceding neighbor on large jumps, and starts preparing smaller jumps too late.

Keep six neighboring rows on both sides during reader movement, using the existing 100 ms movement sample. Invalidate the virtualizer's cached extraction when movement starts, even if a small first wheel event leaves the visible indexes unchanged. Initial tail placement and idle retention limits stay with their existing owners. The production change removes nine lines overall and adds no scheduler or retained state.

## Evidence

Qualification is in progress; this PR is a draft and auto-merge is off.

| Proof | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Typecheck and focused initial-range tests | Passed; five cases cover both directions, cached extraction, and yielding end preparation |
| Independent review | No accepted P0–P2 findings after fixing movement-cache invalidation |
| Committed-head filmstrip, 400 messages | Both endpoints reached. All inspected head frames retain painted transcript content; base repeatedly presents empty areas |
